Andrew Huberman on why Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic are all going to become biotech companies.

"Dario came up through neuroscience. Sam, I've spoken to, is extremely smart about the neuroscience, as is Zuck.

The technologists who used to just engineer stuff, they're becoming neuroscientists...and I think most people don't realize that.

They will all tell you, 'Okay, here's the goal. The goal is to be able to read and write from your brain non-invasively.'

Even just for things like drive and motivation, a non-invasive device where you could literally crank up your level of motivation by stimulating the nucleus accumbens and related pathways while engaging in a particular learning task or in hard work, and then turning it off so that you can capture more energy.

That's coming, and those companies are all about that. That's what the real arms race of AI is about."

In April 2025, U.S. officials accused Chang Guang Satellite Technology, a Chinese company with links to the country’s military-industrial sector, of providing satellite imagery that helped the Houthis target U.S. warships in the Red Sea. Washington raised the issue with Beijing, yet U.S. officials said the assistance continued. China was also buying the overwhelming majority of Iran’s exported oil, providing Tehran with revenue while Chinese companies appeared repeatedly in Houthi procurement networks.
For years, this left the Houthis room to recover from sanctions and military losses. A company could be designated, a shipment intercepted, or a weapons depot destroyed without depriving the Houthis of access to the markets behind them. Today, Operation Economic Fury is making that recovery more difficult by tightening pressure on Iranian oil revenue and the shipping and financial networks that keep it moving. That means the Houthis’ ability to continue replacing what they’ve lost now depends increasingly on a system under pressure of its own—though that pressure is still not sufficient to neutralize them.

https://t.co/v8buSlTEd5

I talk to LPs outside of crypto every single day right now, most of who have nothing to do with this industry. And they don't have the faintest idea how far we've come, what kind of insane tailwinds we have now, or what strong onchain businesses are generating in actual cashflows.

Some of them haven't even heard of stablecoins yet wtf?

When I tell them, it clicks, and they're always pretty impressed. But it's incredible how hard it is to shake the negative association most of them still carry from 2021, 2022, or even earlier. to most of them it's still kind of a scam and darknet industry. They have no idea what's actually going on, literally asking me why we even need so many crypto-"currencies", they will never replace the dollar lol.

So here's the thing: either we're extremely delusional, circle jerking in our own bubble about a supercycle that's never going to happen.

OR we're way earlier in this cycle than even I would have expected.

I'm strongly betting on the latter. and I'm pretty sure that not much is going to change about that until we've broken new ATHs and enter the parabolic zone.

Fun few years ahead.

cash can't be frozen at a distance. stablecoins can. wires - sort of, not really. 

stablecoin issuers are instantly legible to law enforcement. networks of banks and go-betweens arent. 

the people I've talked to that know how stablecoin compliance works AND have experience in conventional illicit finance agree 10 times out of 10 that stablecoins are better for LEO / anti illicit flow purposes. 

has the IRGC used stablecoins? yes, and they've paid the price. could issuers have done more? absolutely. they have been way too conservative with seizures. still miles better than cash or networks of banks and hawala etc. 

anyone that thinks that stables are somehow "worse" for illicit finance enforcement hasn't talked to practitioners enough.

Big Tech is funding the megawatts. I’m watching the companies advancing the pounds. 🔥

The most common pushback I hear on @Collector_Crypt is that it's "jUsT a gAmBLiNg pLaTfOrm" and "gaChA iSnT suStAinAbLe"

It's simply just wrong, and the @Blockworks data proves it:

Start with the chart most people skip. Wallets holding at least one tokenized collectible, and this is with Gachapon wallets excluded. We are at 18,000+ wallets already, and the curve is steepening into October. 

Those wallets hold $28.9M of insured collectibles across 98,235 cards sitting in the vault right now.

More telling: wallets holding more than one card went from 3k to 8k this year. People aren't trying it once and leaving. They're accumulating.

But the strongest signal is redemptions.

Redeeming means burning the NFT and having the physical card shipped to your door. It's the most expensive, least liquid, most committed action available on the platform. A gambler never does this. A gambler flips and moves on.

Redemptions just hit an all-time high of $1.7M in a single week, at roughly $8k average per wallet.

People are taking real cards home, actual collectors do collect.

Then look at what they actually hold. Across 18,202 wallets and 98,235 cards, average card value scales from $52 in the smallest portfolios to $3,451 in the largest. A 66x step-up. Collectors moving up tiers aren't buying more volume, but they're buying better cards. That's exactly what a real collector does.

633 wallets hold a card worth over $1,000. Two hold cards worth $1M. Shout out to @charred_io here.

To sum it up: the gacha has just been the Trojan horse to get enough supply onchain to attract the right collectors. 

What's actually happening though is what's always been the bullcase from day 1: Collector slowly but surely becoming the superior marketplace that collectors trust and collect on.

$STONK is up 513% in the last 30 days, but its revenue pace is down 34%.

The SEC just made token buybacks a lot easier, so I wanted to know which protocols are actually earning more while their tokens lag behind.

I checked 23 revenue tokens across 7 sectors and compared revenue pace to 30D price growth.

Launchpads

- https://t.co/f1pTxLVLNd: Revenue -34% | $STONK +513%
- https://t.co/h9VveifpFO: Revenue -7% | $BONK +19%
- https://t.co/xR4HP5omQ3: Revenue +34% | $PUMP +52%
- Pons: Revenue -66% | $PONS -52%

Chains

- TRON: Revenue -3% | $TRX +2%
- Polygon: Revenue +4% | $POL +13%
- Avalanche: Revenue +51% | $AVAX +46%
- Arbitrum: Revenue +20% | $ARB +54%

DEXs

- Curve: Revenue +69% | $CRV +5%
- Raydium: Revenue -33% | $RAY +145%
- Uniswap: Revenue -33% | $UNI +45%

Perp DEXs

- Hyperliquid: Revenue -12% | $HYPE +10%
- Lighter: Revenue +3% | $LIT -16%
- GMX: Revenue +47% | $GMX +13%

Lending

- Aave: Revenue -1% | $AAVE +38%
- Sky: Revenue -1% | $SKY +39%
- World Liberty: Revenue +4% | $WLFI -2%

Cross-chain

- THORChain: Revenue -5% | $RUNE +62%
- Chainflip: Revenue +40% | $FLIP -26%
- NEAR: Revenue +21% | $NEAR +125%

Liquid staking

- Lido: Revenue +5% | $LDO +22%
- https://t.co/amwOX2ZI2i: Revenue +8% | $ETHFI +37%
- Solv: Revenue +4% | $SOLV +32%

A few of these tokens are pumping while the protocol makes less money.

$STONK is the wildest, but $RAY and $UNI are doing it too:

- $RAY: Revenue -33% | Price +145%
- $UNI: Revenue -33% | Price +45%

And a few are earning way more while the token barely moves:

- $CRV: Revenue +69% | Price +5%
- $GMX: Revenue +47% | Price +13%
- $FLIP: Revenue +40% | Price -26%

None of this means $CRV or $GMX has to go up. 30 days is a short window, and revenue only helps a buyback if it actually flows back to the token.

But if I'm hunting for buyback plays, I'd start with the ones where revenue keeps climbing and price hasn't caught on yet. 

I'd rather dig into those than ape whatever token just announced a buyback.

What revenue tokens are you watching right now?

David Friedberg: The AI Wars Are Already Here, and America Can’t Hit Pause

“We always assumed in the sci-fi novels that we would be in an era of having robot wars, and I think we failed to recognize that the software came first, and we are actually having the AI wars.

I think we will see a massive rise in defense systems. What I heard in DC this week was some Fortune 50 CEOs are very worried about cyber defense.

That means they're going to start to make this their #1 priority to address at the board level. That means the budgets for cyber defense are going to go through the roof.

Now, let me ask you a question. When you have to do cyber defense in an era of AI, are you going to use old school software, or are you going to use AI?

You're going to use AI.

And because of that, because cyber defense is going to need to grow, the US is going to need to provide competitive AI for cyber defense. It is a classic arms race scenario.

And so the US cannot simply step back and pause and turn off AI. It is already everywhere in the world. Therefore, the risks are rising. Therefore, we need to increase our investment in AI to maintain our cyber defense capabilities, both at the enterprise level and at the government level, and potentially even at the civilian consumer level.

So I think that the cyber defense necessity actually mandates that we continue to build out data centers to support it.”
